name: Drought / Water Deficit Stress
summary: Midday leaf rolling or wilting that partially recovers overnight, paired with dry crisp brown leaf margins and cracked soil.

immediateActions: Irrigate deeply at the root zone in early morning or late evening rather than light midday sprinkling.
Apply 5–8 cm of dry rice straw, coconut husk, or grass mulch around bases to cut soil evaporation.
biologicalControl: Incorporate composted organic matter after harvest to raise soil water-holding capacity.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do NOT apply chemical fungicides or granular nitrogen fertilizer while plants are drought-stressed—salts will worsen root burn.
prevention: Use raised-bed mulching, drip/furrow scheduling, and drought-tolerant varieties for dry-season crops.

name: Overwatering / Waterlogging & Root Hypoxia
summary: Plants droop and wilt even though soil is saturated; lower leaves turn uniformly dull yellow, and roots turn dark mushy brown without milky bacterial ooze.

immediateActions: Stop irrigation immediately and dig shallow surface drainage channels to drain standing water away from beds.
Gently aerate crusted topsoil around ridges once surface water recedes.
biologicalControl: Apply Trichoderma-enriched compost once drained to protect weakened roots from opportunistic Pythium/Phytophthora rot.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Avoid extra soil drenches until excess water drains; check stem cut in clear water to rule out Ralstonia bacterial wilt.
prevention: Plant upland vegetables and papaya/pepper on 25–40 cm raised cambered beds ahead of monsoon season.

name: Too Little Sunlight / Shade Etiolation Stress
summary: Thin, pale-green to yellowish leaves with weak, overly stretched tall stems ("leggy" internodes) and poor flower or fruit set under heavy canopy or monsoon cloud cover.

immediateActions: Prune overhanging shade-tree branches or thin overly crowded crop rows to restore direct sunlight.
Stake stretched weak stems gently so they do not lodge in wind.
biologicalControl: Avoid heavy nitrogen applications under shade, which intensify soft leggy growth and fungal susceptibility.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: No pesticide needed—restoring light intensity reverses new leaf pale coloration within 7–10 days.
prevention: Match shade-intolerant crops (maize, tomato, chili, okra) to open sunny blocks; save partial shade for coffee, cacao, or black pepper.

name: Fertilizer Burn / Excess Nitrogen & Salt Toxicity
summary: Uniform crispy brown scorching along leaf tips and outer margins shortly after heavy urea/NPK side-dressing or fresh uncomposted manure, sometimes with white salt crust on dry soil.

immediateActions: Flush the root zone thoroughly with clean freshwater irrigation 2–3 times over 48 hours to leach excess soluble salts below roots.
Scrape away visible clumps of undissolved fertilizer granules sitting directly against plant stems.
biologicalControl: Apply well-aged compost or humic-rich organic mulch once salts are flushed to buffer soil conductivity.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Halt ALL chemical fertilizer and foliar nutrient sprays for at least 2–3 weeks until new roots and leaves recover.
prevention: Split fertilizer doses, keep granules 8–10 cm away from stems, water immediately after application, and age raw manure for 60+ days.

name: Nutrient Deficiency (N / K / Mg / Iron Chlorosis)
summary: Symmetrical yellowing without insect or fungal spore signs: uniform older-leaf yellowing (Nitrogen), scorched older edges (Potassium), or yellow leaf blades with green veins (Magnesium/Iron).

immediateActions: Determine leaf position: older lower leaves indicate mobile N/P/K/Mg deficiency; youngest top leaves indicate immobile Iron/Zinc/Calcium/Boron deficit.
Apply balanced NPK side-dressing or compost tea + wood ash (potassium) watered in cleanly.
biologicalControl: Incorporate vermicompost, green manure legumes, or Azolla/Rhizobium biofertilizers to build long-term nutrient supply.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: For rapid micronutrient correction (Zn/Fe/Mg), apply a light chelated foliar spray at cool morning hours.
prevention: Conduct simple soil pH checks (target pH 5.8–6.8) since acidic soil locks up phosphorus and magnesium even when present.

name: Heat Stress & Sunscald
summary: Bleached papery white-to-tan sunken patches on the sun-facing side of tomato, chili, papaya, or durian fruits and upper leaves during >36°C heatwaves.

immediateActions: Erect temporary 30–40% shade netting over high-value vegetable/nursery beds during peak dry-season heat.
Avoid aggressive leaf pruning that suddenly exposes green fruits to direct afternoon sun.
biologicalControl: Maintain thick organic mulch and steady soil moisture so transpirational leaf cooling stays active.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Avoid spraying sulfur or emulsifiable oils when temperatures exceed 34°C, as they intensify sunscald burn.
prevention: Use calcium-silicate or kaolin clay sun-protectant sprays on sensitive fruit crops in intense dry seasons.

name: Herbicide / Chemical Drift Injury
summary: Cupped, strap-shaped, twisted young shoots (hormone/2,4-D drift) or stark bleached white/yellow bands across leaves (glyphosate/paraquat drift) without insects.

immediateActions: If spray drift happened within the last 1–2 hours, rinse foliage thoroughly with clean water.
Provide light balanced irrigation and seaweed/amino-acid biostimulant to help new uninjured shoots grow out.
biologicalControl: Trim severely distorted dead tips only after new healthy lateral buds begin emerging.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Flush sprayer tanks 3 times with clean water and detergent after herbicide use—never reuse herbicide sprayers for foliar crop sprays.
prevention: Spray weeds only in calm early mornings (<5 km/h wind) using low-pressure drift-guard nozzles and buffer borders.

name: Soil Salinity / Acid-Sulfate & Iron Toxicity
scientificName: Abiotic — Coastal Salt or Acidic Soil Stress
summary: White-tipped scorched leaves and stunted patches in coastal brackish deltas (salinity), or tiny rusty-brown spots coalescing into orange-bronze older rice leaves (acid-sulfate iron toxicity).

immediateActions: For coastal salinity: flush fields with fresh canal/rainwater whenever available and strengthen perimeter bunds against brackish tides.
For flooded rice iron toxicity: drain field intermittently for 3–5 days to oxidize excess ferrous iron in the root zone.
biologicalControl: Apply agricultural lime (CaCO3) or rice-husk biochar + potassium/zinc fertilizers to counteract acidity and iron uptake.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Avoid ammonium sulfate in acid-sulfate soils; prefer urea paired with adequate potassium and phosphorus.
prevention: Plant salt-tolerant or iron-toxicity-tolerant SEA cultivars in delta and peatland zones.

name: Wind / Typhoon / Mechanical Leaf Damage
summary: Clean parallel shredding along banana/maize leaf veins, snapped petioles, or bruised stems after high winds/hail—without caterpillar frass or fungal concentric rings.

immediateActions: Prop upright lodged stalks/banana pseudostems gently and trim cleanly snapped broken branches to prevent secondary rot entry.
Drain standing storm rainwater promptly from beds.
biologicalControl: Apply a light preventive Trichoderma or copper mist on wounded high-value fruit trees (durian, mango, cacao) right after severe hail/typhoons.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do not spray insecticides for shredded wind leaves—check for frass or insects before treating.
prevention: Plant bamboo/Gliricidia windbreak rows around exposed banana, papaya, and orchard plots.
